 7   Q.   What is the purpose of your testimony in this proceeding?

 8   A.   On March 27, 2026, El Paso Electric Company (“Company” or “EPE”) filed an Application

13        use of test year adjustments to project entire generation units into the test year and the large

14        load tariff.

15                My silence on any issue raised by EPE in its case-in-chief should not be construed

17   Q.   Please summarize your testimony and recommendations.

18   A.   The Commission should reject EPE’s proposed adjustment to include the Carne and Santa

          II.   THE METHOD USED TO DIRECTLY ASSIGN COSTS OF RENEWABLE
                     RESOURCES TO NEW MEXICO BY INCLUDING THEM AS
                 ADJUSTMENTS TO AN HISTORICAL TEST YEAR IS NOT JUST AND
                 REASONABLE AND IS CONTRARY TO THE COMMISSION’S RULES
                   REGARDING ADJUSTMENTS FOR HISTORICAL TEST YEARS
 1

 2   Q.    Please explain how El Paso Electric modeled the Santa Teresa Solar + Battery

 3         facility in its filing.

 4   A.    El Paso Electric’s work papers submitted in response to data request CLC 06-01 show that

 5         the Company modeled Santa Teresa as a 150-MW solar facility paired with a 150-MW

 6         battery system, even though only a portion of that capacity is assigned to New Mexico. In

 7         the “Annualized kW and kWh” section of the work papers, the Company states: “Maximum

 8         Interconnected load for Santa Teresa Project is 150 MW… 58 MW of the Santa Teresa

 9         Solar Site are directly assigned to New Mexico to meet the minimum threshold allocation

10         of 172,000 MWhs agreed in NMPRC Case 25-00038-UT.” The work papers further explain

11         that “Monthly weighted capacity factors are used to calculate Test Year Period demand

12         because interval data is not available for these facilities.” These statements demonstrate

13         that EPE annualized Santa Teresa’s output using a weighted capacity factor of

14         approximately 0.363 applied across 8,760 hours, which is a standard method for estimating

15         solar production when interval data is unavailable. At the resource-modeling level, this

16         approach is technically sound and consistent with Commission practice for estimating

17         output from new renewable facilities. A similar methodology was used to project the

18         output of the Carne solar facility.

19   Q.    Does this modeling comply with NMPRC rules governing test-year data?

                                                   3
                                      DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                         TED THOMAS
                                   NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   A.   The modeling itself is not the problem. The Company’s use of weighted capacity factors

 2        to estimate annual energy is permissible under 17.9.530 NMAC, which allows utilities to

 3        incorporate “known and measurable changes” and reasonable estimates when interval data

 4        is not available. The work papers’ statement that monthly weighted capacity factors are

 5        used because interval data is unavailable is consistent with that rule. The compliance issue

 6        arises not from the method of estimating Carne and Santa Teresa’s output, but from the

 7        way in which EPE incorporates both Carne and Santa Teresa into the test-year structure.

 8   Q.   What is the compliance issue with the test-year structure?

 9   A.   The work papers reveal that Carne and Santa Teresa are not base-period resources but

10        future resources. The Company states that Carne and Santa Teresa are “expected to be

11        COD during the rate year.” Under 17.1.3 NMAC, a utility must choose either a historical

12        test year with pro forma adjustments or a future test year with full linkage schedules,

13        adjusted base-period data, and complete explanation of all estimates. EPE’s filing does

14        neither. Instead, the Company inserts Carne and Santa Teresa directly into what it labels

15        the “Test Period,” even though Carne and Santa Teresa were not in service during the base

16        period and their inclusion is not supported by the linkage schedules required for a future

17        test year. This creates a hybrid test year, which the Commission’s rules do not permit.

18   Q.   How do the work papers demonstrate that EPE is using a hybrid test year?

19   A.   The work papers contain a “Base Period” covering October 2024 through September 2025,

20        which includes only existing resources. They then present a “Test Period” for the same

21        dates, but add Santa Teresa, Carne, Felina, and Milagro—each described as “expected to

22        be COD during the rate year.” By embedding future resources directly into the test-year

                                                   4
                                       DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                          TED THOMAS
                                    NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        calculations without providing linkage schedules showing how base-period data is adjusted

 2        to reflect these future additions, EPE has effectively created a future test year in substance

 3        while labeling it as a historical test year. The Commission’s rules require a clear and

 4        consistent test-year framework, and EPE’s approach does not satisfy either framework.

 5   Q.   Why is the absence of linkage schedules a violation of NMPRC rules?

 6   A.   Under 17.1.3.18 NMAC, a future test-year filing must include a complete explanation of

 7        all adjustments, supporting documentation, and linkage schedules showing the derivation

 8        of future test-year amounts. These schedules must demonstrate how the base period

 9        transitions into the future test year, including the effects of new resources, changes in load,

10        and operational adjustments. EPE’s work papers provide none of these required elements.

11        They simply insert Santa Teresa’s 58 MW of solar and 50 MW of battery capacity into the

12        test-year demand and energy calculations without showing how the base period is adjusted,

13        how Santa Teresa’s COD date affects monthly output, or how battery discharge is modeled.

14        The Company’s own note—“Calculating Santa Teresa as a whole to calculate Battery

15        Discharge and then assigning 50 MW or 1/3 to NM”—acknowledges that a modeling step

16        exists, but the work papers do not contain the required linkage or explanation. This

17        omission violates the future test-year requirements of 17.1.3 NMAC. This also applies to

18        the Carne solar unit.

19   Q.   Does EPE’s dedicated resource assignment for Carne and Santa Teresa comply with

20        Commission rules and orders?

21   A.   No. The work papers states that 58 MW of Santa Teresa’s solar capacity is assigned to New

22        Mexico “to meet the minimum threshold allocation of 172,000 MWhs agreed in NMPRC

                                                    5

                                             TED THOMAS
                                       NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1           Case 25-00038-UT.” This shows that the assignment is driven by a regulatory target rather

 2           than actual test-year operational conditions. However, that target is not consistent with the

 3           relevant regulatory order. In NMPRC Case No. 25-00038-UT, the Commission approved

 4           assigning the entire energy production of the Santa Teresa 150-MW solar facility to the

 5           New Mexico jurisdiction, along with 50 MW of the total 150 MW of battery energy storage

 6           system (“BESS”) capacity. While NMPRC Staff and EPE appear to have agreed that a

 7           minimum allocation of 172,000 MWhs of Santa Teresa solar energy production would be

 8           necessary for the Santa Teresa Project to satisfy the Reasonable Cost Threshold or RCT

 9           under the Renewable Energy Act in conjunction with the 50 MW of BESS that EPE

10           proposed dedicating to New Mexico in Case No. 25-00038-UT, the Commission’s final

11           order flatly provided for EPE to assign all of the Santa Teresa Project’s solar production to

12           New Mexico indefinitely and required EPE to file any request to alter the allocation of the

13           energy from the Santa Teresa Project between Texas and New Mexico in a separate

14           docket. 1 EPE did not request a reduction from the 150 MW allocation of Santa Teresa

15           solar production in its most recent annual Renewable Energy Act plan application, NMPRC

16           Docket No. 26-0000093, and has not made such a request in a stand-alone docket

17           concerning the Santa Teresa Project alone.

18

19           Under 17.9.530 NMAC, dedicated resource assignments must reflect actual test-year

20           conditions, not policy thresholds as interpreted, or misinterpreted, by the utility. Because

 1        Santa Teresa was not in service during the base period and because its proposed

 2        jurisdictional energy allocation in this case is based on a minimum MWh requirement

 3        rather than operational data—or upon the jurisdictional allocation of 100% of the Santa

 4        Teresa project’s projected solar energy production as has            been authorized by the

 5        Commission—the Company’s proposed assignment cannot be incorporated into a

 6        historical test year without violating the requirement that test-year data reflect actual

 7        operations. Carne did not have a maximum output set regulatorily, but its output was also

 8        modeled in a manner inconsistent with the Commission’s rules for future test years.

 9   Q.   Based on these facts, how should the Commission treat EPE’s filing?

10   A.   The Commission should treat EPE’s filing as a future test-year case. The Company’s own

11        work papers show that Santa Teresa, Carne, Felina, and Milagro are future resources

12        expected to be in service during the rate year. By incorporating these resources directly

13        into the test-year demand and energy calculations, EPE has made future conditions an

14        integral part of its test-year model. Under 17.1.3 NMAC, once a utility incorporates future

15        resources into its test-year calculations, the filing is a future test-year case and must comply

16        with the future test-year requirements, including linkage schedules, adjusted base-period

17        data, and full explanation of all estimates. EPE has not provided these required elements.

18        Therefore, the filing cannot be treated as a historical test-year case and must be evaluated

19        under the future test-year rules. The Commission should require EPE to provide the

20        missing linkage schedules and supporting documentation or, alternatively, reject the

21        test-year structure as non-compliant.

 1   Q.     What data did El Paso Electric use to project the output of the Santa Teresa Solar +

 2          Battery facility?

 3   A.     The Company’s work papers make clear that Santa Teresa’s projected output is not based

 4          on any operational data from Santa Teresa itself, because the facility was not yet in service

 5          and therefore has no interval data. Instead, El Paso Electric substitutes the monthly

 6          weighted capacity factors from the Buena Vista Facility 2 as the proxy for Santa Teresa’s

 7          solar performance. This substitution is explicitly stated in the work papers’ notes, where

 8          the Company writes: “(b) Capacity factors for the Buena Vista Facility 2 are used to

 9          calculate Test Year Period demand either because interval data is limited or not available

10          for these facilities.” 2 Santa Teresa is one of the facilities marked with the “(b)” designation,

11          and therefore its solar output is projected using the Buena Vista 2 capacity-factor profile.

12                  The work papers also assign Santa Teresa a weighted annual capacity factor of

13          0.36299999999999999, which corresponds to the Buena Vista 2 profile rather than any

14          Santa Teresa-specific measurement. The Company then applies this Buena Vista-derived

15          capacity factor to a New Mexico jurisdictional assignment of 58 MW of solar capacity that

16          does not conform with actual regulatory authorization, multiplying it across 8,760 hours to

17          produce the Company’s annualized energy estimate. In other words, Santa Teresa’s

18          projected output is entirely derived from Buena Vista 2’s historical performance, not from

19          Santa Teresa’s own operational characteristics. This is also true with respect to the Carne

20          solar facility.

 1   Q.          Why is the use of Buena Vista 2 data significant for evaluating the Company’s

 2              test-year compliance?

 3   A.         The use of Buena Vista 2’s capacity-factor data to project Santa Teresa’s output is

 4              significant because it confirms that Santa Teresa is being modeled as a future resource

 5              rather than a base-period resource. The work papers acknowledge that Santa Teresa is

 6              “expected to be COD during the rate year,” meaning it was not in service during the base

 7              period and has no interval data of its own. 3 Under 17.1.3 NMAC, once a utility incorporates

 8              future resources into its test-year calculations, the filing must be treated as a future test-year

 9              case and must include linkage schedules, adjusted base-period data, and full explanation of

10              all estimates. The Company’s reliance on Buena Vista 2 data for the Santa Teresa Project

11              is therefore not merely a modeling choice; it is evidence that Santa Teresa is being treated

12              as a future test-year adjustment.

13                        The Commission’s rules require that future test-year estimates be supported by

14              linkage schedules showing how the base period transitions into the future test year. In this

15              case, the work papers provide no such linkage. They simply insert Santa Teresa’s 58 MW

16              of solar (per EPE) and 50 MW of battery capacity into the test-year demand and energy

17              calculations, using Buena Vista 2’s capacity factors as a proxy. The absence of linkage

18              schedules and explanatory support means the filing does not comply with the future

19              test-year requirements of 17.1.3.18 NMAC.

 1   Q.       How does this substitution affect the Commission’s evaluation of the Company’s

 2            test-year structure?

 3   A.       The substitution of Buena Vista 2 capacity-factor data for Santa Teresa’s output

 4            demonstrates that the Company is not presenting a historical test year. A historical test year

 5            must reflect actual operations during the test-year period, and Santa Teresa did not operate

 6            during that period. By using Buena Vista 2’s historical performance to estimate Santa

 7            Teresa’s future output, the Company is making a future-test-year adjustment. Under

 8            Commission rules, once a utility makes such an adjustment, it must provide the full

 9            future-test-year framework, including linkage schedules and adjusted base-period data.

10            Because El Paso Electric has not provided these required elements, the filing cannot be

11            treated as a historical test-year case.

12                      The work papers’ own language confirms this future-test-year posture. The

13            Company states that Santa Teresa is “expected to be COD during the rate year,” and that

14            Buena Vista 2’s capacity factors are used “because interval data is limited or not

15            available.” 4 These statements show that the Company is projecting future operations rather

16            than reporting historical ones. As a result, the Commission must treat the filing as a future

17            test-year case and require the Company to provide the missing linkage schedules and

18            supporting documentation required by 17.1.3 NMAC.

19   Q.       What is your conclusion regarding the Company’s use of Buena Vista 2 data to

20            project Santa Teresa’s output?

13   Q.       Was the issue regarding improper use of a hybrid test year raised by motion and ruled

14            upon by the Hearing Examiners in this proceeding?

15   A.       Yes, on September 26, 2026, Hearing Examiners Rossi and Gedko denied the City of Las

16            Cruces’s motion to dismiss the case. The basis of the motion was the mixing of a Future

17            Test Year Period with respect to generation units not in service during the Historical Test

18            Period with what otherwise was purported to be a Historical Test Period application. The

19            Hearing Examiners found that “Instead, under a ‘Historical Test Year Period’ filing under

20            17.9.530.7(S)(1), the ‘Historical Test Year Period’ which establishes the utility’s total

21            revenue requirement is developed by applying to the Base Period ‘all proper adjustments,

 1           such as annualization and known and measurable changes.’ CLC’s concerns regarding the

 2           proper accounting for post-test-period resource additions, and their relationship to test

 3           period load, are therefore properly the subject of testimony and litigation regarding ‘proper

 4           adjustments, such as known and measurable changes’ to the Base Period defined in EPE’s

 5           Application and Amended Application, filed under 17.9.530 NMAC.” 6

 6   Q.      Why do you offer a position that was rejected by the Hearing Examiners?

 7   A.      First, the Commission should revisit the question resolved by the Hearing Examiners and

 8           either dismiss the case as requested in the motion or deny cost recovery for the generation

 9           units not in service during the historical test period. Should the Commission affirm the

10           ruling on the motion, the Hearing Examiners made it clear that this is a historical test year

11           rate application, thus EPE is seeking to use adjustments to a historical test year to project

12           into existence entirely new generation facilities for rate recovery purposes. This is contrary

13           to the Commission’ rules regarding historical test year rate applications.

14   Q.      What does the Commission’s rule require when a utility elects to use a historical test

15           year?

16   A.      When a utility elects a historical test year, the Commission requires that the test year consist

17           of actual data from a twelve-month base period. The rule permits adjustments only to

18           annualize, normalize, or reflect known and measurable changes. The problem with EPE's

19           treatment of the new generation resources is therefore not merely that those resources were

20           not operating during the Base Period. The issue is whether EPE may adjust historical

 1        experience to include the costs and modeled output of new generation expected to be

 2        operating when rates take effect, while failing to make corresponding adjustments for the

 3        load, billing determinants, and revenues associated with the conditions giving rise to that

 4        additional generation. Such one-sided adjustments risk producing a Test Year that does not

 5        consistently represent the conditions on which the proposed rates are based.

 6        This structure ensures that historical test year filings remain grounded in verifiable

7         operational experience rather than forecasts or hypothetical projections.

8    Q.   How does this rule apply to a new generation facility that was not in service during

9         the base period?

10   A.   A new generation facility that was not in service during the base period should not be

11        included in a historical test year through a known and measurable adjustment because its

12        costs, dispatch profile, and usage characteristics did not occur within the base period. The

13        facility’s future operation is not a known and measurable change; it is a forecasted

14        condition.

15   Q.   Are new generation facilities treated differently under the Commission’s rules?

16   A.   Yes. A plant that enters service after the base period is, by definition, a major plant

17        addition. Its costs and operational characteristics must be evaluated through the future test

18        year framework, which requires linkage data, justification of assumptions, and a

19        demonstration of how projected conditions relate to the historical base period. The

20        Commission has deliberately separated the treatment of actual historical data from

21        forecasted future conditions, and new generation facilities fall squarely within the latter

22        category.

 1   Q.    What would be the regulatory consequence if a utility attempted to include projected

 2         usage of a new facility in a historical test year?

 3   A.    If a utility attempted to include projected usage of a new facility in a historical test year, it

 4         would undermine the regulatory distinction between actual and forecasted data. It would

 5         effectively convert the filing into a future test year case without providing the linkage data,

 6         cost drivers, and justification required under the future test year rule. Such an approach

 7         would deprive the Commission of the structured review that future test year filings are

 8         designed to provide and would violate the Commission’s test-year framework.

 9   Q.    Based on the Commission’s rules, what is your conclusion?

10   A.    My conclusion is that a utility using a historical test year may not use known and

11         measurable changes to project the usage of a new generation facility that was not in service

12         during the base period. The Commission’s rules require that new plant additions be

13         addressed through the future test year mechanism, and any attempt to incorporate them into

14         a historical test year is inconsistent with both the letter and the purpose of the

15         Commission’s regulations. The Commission should reject the adjustments and deny cost

16         recovery for the generation units EPE seeks to project into existence during the test year.

17         Specifically, the Commission should reject the adjustments proposed in SCHEDULE A-

 1   Q.       Please explain how Test Year energy was determined for use in EPE’s cost-of-service

 2            and rate design models.

 3   A.       Test Year energy is derived directly from the Company’s billed energy during the Base

 4            Period and Historical Test Year ending September 30, 2025. As EPE witness Enedina Soto

 5            explains, “Energy for each jurisdiction is based on billed energy, adjusted for losses.” 8 This

 6            billed energy represents the actual metered consumption recorded for all retail customers

 7            and serves as the foundational input for jurisdictional allocation, class allocation, and

 8            revenue normalization. The Company does not replace billed energy with modeled or

 9            hypothetical values; instead, it begins with the actual billing system data and applies

10            adjustments required by Commission rules and prior rate-case precedent.

11   Q.       How is billed energy converted into the generation-level energy used in allocators and

12            cost assignment?

13   A.       Billed energy is grossed up using the most recent system loss study sponsored by Ms. Soto.

14            She testifies that “both energy and demand allocators take losses into account to

15            appropriately reflect generation ‘at the source’.” 9 This conversion ensures that the

16            allocators reflect the total energy that must be generated to serve retail load, rather than

17            only the energy measured at the customer meter. Loss factors vary by voltage level, and

18            the updated loss study is applied uniformly across all classes to produce generation-level

19            energy values for allocator development.

 1   Q.      Were any jurisdiction-specific adjustments made to Test Year energy?

 2   A.      Yes. The Company made a jurisdictional adjustment to remove the output of dedicated

 3           generation resources from the retail energy used in the allocators. Ms. Soto explains that

 4           “generation from EPE’s resources that are assigned to serve customers from a specific

 5           jurisdiction were directly assigned to the relevant jurisdiction and removed from the retail

 6           customers’ energy and demand usage used in the jurisdictional allocators.” 10 For example,

 7           Newman Unit 6 is assigned to Texas, and the Carne Solar Project is assigned to New

 8           Mexico. This adjustment does not alter the billed energy itself; rather, it ensures that the

 9           allocators properly reflect the jurisdictional responsibility for dedicated resources.

10   Q.      If directly assigned costs are removed from the cost-of-service study, how do they

11           ultimately get charged to ratepayers?

12   A.      Directly assigned costs reach ratepayers through jurisdiction-specific rate recovery

13           mechanisms, even when they are not included in the cost-of-service allocator model.

14           Directly assigned resources bypass the allocator framework entirely. Their costs do not

15           flow through production, transmission, or distribution allocators. Instead, they are placed

16           directly   into   the    jurisdictional   revenue   requirement   and    recovered       through

17           jurisdiction-specific rates. In this case, the adjustment to add Carne and Santa Teresa

18           capacity costs into the test year appears in EPE’s Schedule A-03, page 3 of 7, as an

19           adjustment to “Other Power Supply Expenses.”

 1   Q.      Did the Company make any adjustments to Test Year energy related to distributed

 2           generation (DG) customers?

3    A.      Yes, but only for allocator purposes. Historically, EPE increased DG customers’ billed

4            energy by substituting delivered energy for net energy. In this case, EPE changed that

5            practice. Ms. Soto testifies that “for the current rate case, EPE did not include the DG

6            Adjustment in its calculation of the production and transmission allocation factors but did

 7           include it in its calculation of the distribution allocators.” 11 She further explains that the

 8           production and transmission allocators now “rely on DG customers’ net energy as opposed

 9           to delivered energy.”⁵ This change affects only the allocation of costs, not the underlying

10           billed energy used for revenue normalization or forecasting.

11   Q.      Was Test Year billed energy adjusted for known and measurable changes?

12   A.      Yes. EPE witness Steven Sierra confirms that Base Period book balances, including billing

13           determinants, were adjusted to reflect “annualization, known and measurable changes, and

14           pro forma adjustments for plant-in-service additions to arrive at Historical Test Year Period

15           amounts.” 12 These adjustments include customer growth, rate schedule changes, and other

16           measurable changes occurring during the Test Year. The adjustments do not replace billed

17           energy; rather, they refine it to ensure that the Test Year reflects conditions expected to
